facts.claim: A large-model finding: Lee and colleagues (2021) found one 61-word sentence repeated over 60,000 times in a common web dataset (C4), and that over 1% of what models trained on such data wrote unprompted was copied word for word from their training text.

A real-model finding: Carlini and colleagues (The Secret Sharer, 2019) planted made-up secrets, canaries, in training text to measure how easily they could be guessed back. From models trained without care for memorisation, they pulled out unique secrets such as credit card numbers.

A large-model finding: Carlini and colleagues (2021) pulled hundreds of training sequences, word for word, out of GPT-2 by prompting it, names, phone numbers and email addresses among them, each in just one document of its training text. Larger models were more vulnerable.

A large-model finding: Kandpal, Wallace and Raffel (2022) found a sequence present 10 times in training is generated about 1,000 times more often than one present once, and that removing duplicates makes models far harder to pull training text from.

A large-model finding: Ippolito and colleagues (2022) built a filter that blocks every reply copying training text word for word, and showed that slightly changed prompts, asking for the text in another style, still got memorised text past it.

A large-model finding: Nasr and colleagues (2023) pulled gigabytes of training text out of open models, and made ChatGPT, tuned to behave as a careful assistant, give out training text 150 times more often than when it behaved normally: the tuning had not removed what it memorised.

A large-model finding: Lukas and colleagues (2023) found that scrubbing personal details out of training text cuts the risk of a model leaking them but doesn’t stop it: real scrubbers miss some, and scrubbing more also strips useful text.
Abadi and colleagues (2016) showed deep networks can be trained with differential privacy, a method that caps how much any one training example can change the model, at a manageable cost in quality.
